title: Pay only for days worked and shelved records
summary: He learned he was paid only for days worked with expenses on him, did not reach $100 until 1938-39, and unreleased records went unpaid.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: How did that compare with what the
other musicians in the band were making at the time?

Oh, they were -- most of them, see, with our tips, with our movies, with our records, by that time I'd made a couple records, with the Quality Serenaders, and $70.00 a week, that was nothing. Of course, that was the beginning of many, many, many surprises. The first one was I didn't know -- I thought that when you joined a band of that caliber, you made your salary plus expenses, plus you made it every week, work or play. I didn't know that you made that $70.00 the days you worked, and only got paid for -- like if you worked three days, you got three-sevenths. And all expenses were on you. I didn't know that, so that started my real, real life.
So how long before you got an adjustment in your salary?
I would say it was a couple of years.
You had to exist on that for a couple of years?

Yeah. Well, I had a little bank account, which I took with me. And it was about a couple of years. I really didn't get above $100.00 a week until about '38, or '39. Of course, along in between there were times when you made a -- like if you made a movie, you had to get the union scale. So you got that. Little things added up. And you made records. Well, they had a plan where you made a record, three for $25.00, three records. So -- well, that's another story. I'm writing
Regardless of how long a recording session took, it was how many records you produced?

They didn't have a time limit in those days. I mean, now the sessions are three hours. Well, no, you just made the record, you know, until it was satisfactory. And then at the end of it, if they didn't like the record, or it didn't sound like what they wanted, they put it on a shelf, and you didn't get paid.

No, you wouldn't get paid. So many of the shelf numbers have been edited later on, and nobody got paid. The music business was the first -- that was the first time I'd ever been sort of, what do you call it, disappointed in the music business. And from then on, it's another story.
